newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - German recovery little help to jobless.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - German recovery little help to jobless.

text.p: Germany will slowly recover from a prolonged economic slump this year and next but stronger growth will do little to alleviate the nation's high unemployment, a survey of economists issued on Wednesday said.

Some 34 economists polled by Reuters said on average that they expected Germany's gross domestic product to grow around 2.2 percent in 1997 and 1.2 percent this year, a steady if unspectactular improvement in economic output.
"Next year we will see moderate growth, initially led by exports and then by domestic factors," said Mathias Haffner, economist at BZW in Frankfurt.
But a stronger economy will do little for Germany's near record level of unemployed with high labour costs and excess capacity discouraging employers from adding workers.

German jobless rates are unlikely to fall much below the psychologically-important ten percent level in 1996 and 1997, the survey showed, with some analysts forecasting rates of 10.5 percent by the end of 1997.
Indeed, most saw only a slight decrease in unemployment this year with joblessness falling to 10.3 percent from September's 10.4 percent.
The economists said they expect Germany's powerful Bundesbank to do its bit to help recovery, keeping the discount rate around its historic low 2.5 percent in the mid-term.

"The Bundesbank's policy is really unusually expansive at the moment and there will come a time next year when this will have to be normalised," said Thomas Kull, economist at Westdeutsche Labndesbank in Duesseldorf.
The survey of 29 economists showed that 13 expect the floor discount rate would rise to three percent in the last quarter of 1997, with six more seeing that level reached in early 1998.
The median forecast for the Lombard rate, the ceiling on German interest rates and now at 4.50 percent, predicted a rise to five percent in the first quarter of 1998.

The Bundesbank has kept its headline rates on hold since April, when it shaved 50 basis points off both. The move was viewed by many observers as the last major easing in the current cycle and as heralding the first German official rate rise since July 1992.

A parallel poll on expectations for German inflation showed that an average of 33 forecasts saw a gradual acceleration in consumer price growth to around two percent by the end of 1997. The Bundesbank is keen to keep inflation below two percent.
One of the key factor's behind Germany's anticipated export-led recovery will be a weaker mark, reducing the price for German goods sold abroad.
The survey showed that fears about European monetary union and relatively sluggish German growth promise to leave the mark weaker against major currencies over the next two years.
According to the poll, the mark is likely to fall to 1.5519 against the dollar by the third quarter of 1998 from 1.5330 now and will slip to 70.00 against the yen from 71.98.
"The mark is going down, down, down," said Holger Schmieding, economist at Merrill Lynch in Frankfurt.
German Bund yields are expected to end the year above their current levels and then continue to rise steadily into 1997 as an economic recovery in Germany finally kicks in, analysts said.
A survey of 33 economists for their forecasts on the 10-year benchmark German Bund yield showed all but two said they saw the yield at six percent or over by the end of 1996.
The yield on the 10-year Bund currently stands just under the six percent level.
